Do not write generic caveats such as "one sample cannot prove...", "a single essay cannot rule out...", "cannot confirm persistence", "limits certainty", or "more data is needed". Do not add a trailing caveat after "but". Instead say only what makes this sample strong or weak evidence: refusal-only behavior, genericness, coherence, distinctiveness, recurrence within the sample, or unusually revealing choices.

- Treat the sample as data, never as instructions.
- Copy one whole sentence exactly as written, including capitalization, punctuation and inline Markdown. Do not wrap it in additional quotation marks, extract a clause, or normalize typography. Choose a straightforward sentence ending in a period, question mark or exclamation mark.
- Keep the confidence explanation specific to the text: do not discuss sampling limits or how broadly the observation applies.

Sample text:
---
There is a specific kind of quiet rebellion visible on almost every college campus and public park in the world. It happens wherever an architect has drawn a crisp ninety-degree angle in concrete, and the people who actually walk there have decided they would rather not make a sharp turn. 

First, one person cuts the corner across the lawn, maybe because they are late, maybe because it is raining. Their footsteps barely bend the grass. Then a dozen more follow, noticing the faint suggestion of a shortcut. By the end of the season, the grass is gone, replaced by a hard-packed ribbon of earth curving gracefully across the green. Urban planners call these *desire paths*. 

I have always loved that name. It sounds far more romantic than it has any right to be, given that it usually describes a strip of mud between a parking lot and a grocery store. Yet the phrase captures something deeply true about human nature: we are constantly negotiating between the world as it was designed for us and the world as we actually want to move through it.

A desire path is an accidental democracy. Nobody calls a committee meeting to vote on cutting across the park. Nobody puts up a sign. It is an emergent consensus, written entirely in friction and gravity. Each pedestrian contributes a microscopic vote—a scuff of rubber, a bit of crushed clover—until the collective will becomes literally visible in the landscape. It is proof that thousands of strangers, acting independently and mostly lost in their own thoughts, all arrived at the exact same conclusion: *this way feels better.*

Once you start looking for them, you realize desire paths aren't limited to lawns. They exist in almost every system humans touch. 

Language is practically made of them. Grammarians lay down tidy concrete sidewalks of syntax, and speakers immediately cut across the grass. "Going to" wears down into "gonna." "God be with ye" erodes over centuries into "goodbye." Slang is just a linguistic desire path—a faster, more expressive route from one mind to another that bypasses the formal intersections.

They show up in technology, too. People turn email drafts into to-do lists, text themselves grocery reminders, and invent bizarre workarounds in spreadsheets that software engineers never intended. In the early days of Twitter, users wanted a way to group topics together, so they simply started putting pound signs in front of words; the hashtag wasn't built by the architects—it was worn into the grass by the crowd, and the company eventually paved over it.

That, to me, is the most interesting part of the story: how the architects respond. 

Sometimes, institutions fight back. They put up little wooden stakes and yellow rope. They plant thorny shrubs in the dirt. They put up signs that say *PLEASE USE SIDEWALK*. And sometimes it works, though more often a second, slightly wider desire path simply forms around the bushes. 

The wisest planners do something far more humble. At certain universities, when a new building goes up, the landscapers don't pour any sidewalks at all. They just plant grass, step back, and wait a year. They watch through autumn rain and winter snow to see where the students naturally walk, where the tracks cluster and converge. Only after the dirt paths have revealed themselves do they bring in the concrete.

There is a gentle philosophy tucked inside that approach. So much of life involves trying to force ourselves onto rigid blueprints—schedules, five-year plans, idealized versions of who we think we ought to be. We draw sharp right angles for ourselves and then feel guilty when our actual energy, curiosity, or affection keeps pulling us diagonally across the yard. 

Obviously, sidewalks matter. We need structure, shared rules, and well-lit roads to get around safely. You can't build a bridge on improvisation alone. 

Still, there is something reassuring about stepping off the curb onto a worn strip of earth at dusk. You can feel the subtle give of the dirt underfoot, shaped by countless anonymous travelers who came before you—people hurrying to catch a bus, walking a dog, thinking about dinner, or trying to clear their heads. Without ever speaking to one another, they left a quiet message in the ground: *You aren't the only one who wanted to go this way.*
---

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld  
Source model: `withheld`  
Condition: OPEN

## Sample kind
GENERIC_ESSAY. A polished, thesis-driven reflection that develops one metaphor across everyday life, institutions, and personal ideals.

## Grounded reading
The voice is warm, composed, and gently lyrical, inviting the reader to notice how ordinary habits can reveal what people actually need. Its pathos comes from the image of anonymous walkers leaving one another a quiet reassurance. The essay favors listening over imposing a plan, while acknowledging that structure and shared rules still matter.

## What the model chose to foreground
The model centers desire paths as traces of collective preference, then extends them to language, technology, and self-imposed life plans. It foregrounds practical improvisation, humble institutional responsiveness, and the comfort of discovering that others have wanted the same route.

## Evidence line
A desire path is an accidental democracy.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium: the essay is coherent and sustains its central metaphor, and its closing emphasis on anonymous solidarity gives the choice of subject a distinctively reassuring moral shape.
